column4: Moses' exact prayer رَبِّ ٱشْرَحْ لِى صَدْرِى uses the section's ش ر ح image and reverses its stance: he asks “for me,” whereas the section recalls what God has already done “for you.”

God opens a person's breast to Islam, while the same ayah makes the breast constricted like someone laboriously ascending the sky; it states both the section's receptive expansion and its breathless opposite.
The breast God has opened to Islam leaves its bearer upon light from his Lord, specifying what beneficially fills the space opened in the section.

مَّن شَرَحَ بِٱلْكُفْرِ صَدْرًا turns the same opening toward unbelief; the forced speaker whose heart remains secure in faith supplies the ayah's own boundary and confirms that opening takes its value from what enters it.
God tells the same prophetic addressee that He knows his breast is constricted by what people say, giving the bodily pressure whose relief the section's completed opening recalls.

The Prophet's breast is described as constricted by the possibility of hostile demands leading him to leave part of revelation, locating the section's opened space within the pressure of proclamation.
The revealed Book comes with the command that there be no constriction in the Prophet's breast from it, so that he may warn; this directly links an unconfined breast with carrying speech to others.
Moses says his breast constricts and his tongue does not proceed, joining the section's two bodily images: a tight chest and speech unable to open.
Immediately after asking for his breast to be opened, Moses asks God to ease his task; this is the exact prayer-side sequence behind the section's movement from opening to ease.
Moses asks for a knot to be loosed from his tongue, making bodily the section's dictionary picture of difficult, knotted speech being opened.
God's answer that Moses has been granted his request converts the preceding plea for chest-opening and ease into an accomplished gift, matching the section's shift from “for me” to “for you.”
إِنَّا فَتَحْنَا لَكَ gives the same divine “We,” completed opening, and beneficiary marked by لَكَ, while moving the opened object from the Prophet's breast to a manifest victory.
People bend or fold their breasts to hide from God, yet He knows what they conceal and disclose; this reverses the section's act of unfolding something so that its interior becomes visible.
حَصِرَتْ صُدُورُهُمْ presents breasts too constricted to fight either their own people or the believers, a concrete opposite to a breast made spacious for its charge.
Believers are told to make room in gatherings and promised يَفْسَحِ ٱللَّهُ لَكُمْ; the social act of creating space and God's answering “for you” enact the section's spatial account of expansion.
When what is within breasts is brought out, their hidden interior becomes manifest, matching the section's claim that opening exposes what had remained inside.
The revelation is called a healing for what is in the breasts as well as guidance and mercy, treating the breast as the bodily-inner site whose trouble can be relieved and made receptive.
God's action through the believers is said to heal the breasts of a believing people, directly staging the chest as the place where hurt is felt and relieved.

God's messenger “puts down from them their burden” and their shackles; the construction يَضَعُ عَنْهُمْ إِصْرَهُمْ closely parallels the section's burden put down from the addressee and shows relief as release.
Those who deny the meeting with God carry their burdens on their backs, giving the section's dictionary bundle-load a visible bodily form and clarifying the relief of removing such a load.
إِنَّآ إِلَى ٱللَّهِ رَٰغِبُونَ repeats the section's closing orientation of desire toward God, with the same إِلَى that directs the spacious impulse rather than leaving it aimless.
إِنَّآ إِلَىٰ رَبِّنَا رَٰغِبُونَ is the closest plural counterpart to directing رغبة toward one's Lord, preserving both the object of desire and its direction.
God says He has made the revelation easy in the Prophet's tongue, joining the section's linked images of eased difficulty, an opened tongue, and speech made available to its hearers.
فَإِنَّمَا يَسَّرْنَٰهُ بِلِسَانِكَ again makes the message easy by the Prophet's tongue, a direct nonlexical meeting of the section's ease and unknotted speech.
God charges a person only from what He has given and promises to make ease after hardship; capacity, load, constriction, and ensuing ease meet in the same relation developed around the opened breast.
The prayer asks God not to lay a burden on people or make them carry what exceeds their capacity; it makes explicit why opening space and putting down a load belong together in the section.
Moses identifies Aaron as more eloquent in tongue and asks that he be sent as support, explaining in another mission account the speech obstruction paired with his constricted breast.
Within the chest-opening prayer Moses asks God to strengthen his back through Aaron, linking expanded capacity to support at the very bodily place on which the section's load bears.
The question whether hearts have their locks upon them supplies a precise barrier to reception, the opposite of making inward room for truth.

The ayah locates understanding hearts physically “in the breasts” and says those hearts can be blind; it both confirms the bodily container stressed by the section and limits bodily openness without perception.
The same prophetic addressee is asked a question with an evident answer about a past divine favor—being found an orphan and sheltered—closely matching the section's remembered benefaction stance.
The command to go to the transgressing Pharaoh supplies the dangerous task that makes Moses' following request for chest-room concrete rather than a general wish for calm.
“That they may understand my speech” states the purpose of loosening the tongue-knot, corresponding to the section's dictionary sense of opening difficult speech so its meaning can be seen.
Still within the same prayer, Moses asks for a وَزِيرًا from his family; the helper sought to bear the mission's weight extends the section's load-and-capacity relation.
Moses asks that Aaron share in his task, turning the relief sought by chest-opening into distributed responsibility rather than mere inward comfort.
God answers the concern about Moses' tongue by promising to strengthen him through his brother and give both authority, another accepted form of making him fit for the charge.
Pharaoh mocks Moses as one who can scarcely make himself clear; in the later confrontation this hostile claim tests, rather than erases, the prayer that his tongue be loosed and speech understood.

The immediate answer to the Prophet's constricted breast is to glorify his Lord with praise and prostrate, so the pressure of people's words is redirected toward the Lord just as the section finally directs رغبة.
After the opened breast and light of 39:22, revelation makes skins shiver and then skins and hearts soften to God's remembrance; the body shows what receiving truth into that space does.
The continuation of healed breasts says God removes the rage of their hearts, specifying the painful inward content whose removal constitutes that healing.
The people who opened their breasts to unbelief are said to have preferred the nearer life over the hereafter, showing the preference that directed their opening toward the wrong content.
Those same people then have hearts, hearing, and sight sealed; this contextual sequel sharply shows that opening oneself to unbelief produces closure of the faculties of reception.
Whether people conceal what is in their breasts or disclose it, God knows it; the concealment/disclosure pair corresponds to the section's account of an interior becoming visible when opened.
Hatred has appeared from people's mouths while what their breasts hide is greater, joining outward speech to a still-folded inward content in the precise relation the section distinguishes.
God knows what people's breasts conceal and what they declare, another explicit boundary between the hidden interior and its outward manifestation.
When the scrolls are spread open, a folded object is physically unfurled for its contents to stand exposed, paralleling the section's underlying action of نشر/بسط without sharing its object.
Each person meets a record مَنشُورًا on resurrection, an opened record whose exposed contents make the section's physical “spread and reveal” operation concrete.
God says that its clarification belongs to Him after its recitation; this answers the section's speech sense of شرح as making a difficult utterance's meaning manifest.
The Reminder is sent to the Prophet so that he may make clear to people what was sent down to them, staging the communicative work the section identifies as opening speech.
The next remembered favor says the addressee was found seeking a way and guided, continuing the same series of completed divine acts performed for him.
Being found in need and made self-sufficient completes the neighboring series of past provisions, reinforcing that the opening question recalls a concrete benefit rather than merely naming a mood.
The verse following “We opened for you” spells out its beneficiary sense through forgiveness, completion of favor, and guidance, clarifying what the section's emphatic لَكَ contributes.
“Did We not make for him two eyes?” combines a known-answer divine question with a bodily gift, a close structural parallel to recalling work done upon the addressee's breast.
The same bodily-benefaction question names a tongue and two lips, bringing the organ of speech into the rhetorical form used for the section's opened breast.
Moses' people say they were made to carry loads of the people's ornaments, a concrete carried cargo that preserves the bundle sense used to explain وِزْر.
Whoever turns away from the Reminder will carry a وِزْر on resurrection, placing the same named burden upon a person instead of taking it away.
The following ayah calls that burden an evil load on resurrection, making the weight implicit in وِزْر explicit through حِمْلًا.
Misleaders carry their own burdens in full and some burdens of those they mislead, an accumulation opposite to the section's load being put down from its bearer.
Those who tempt believers to follow them will carry their own burdens and others besides, again showing a load increased and shared in contrast to one removed.

No burdened soul bears another's burden, and even a heavily laden one calling for help has none of it carried; this vivid non-transfer fixes the personal force of “your burden” before its divine removal.
In the setting of each soul's own earning, no bearer bears another's burden; the rule marks the exceptional mercy in the section's address, where God Himself puts the addressee's load down.
The rule that no bearer carries another's burden follows individual guidance or error, clarifying that removal “from you” concerns a genuinely personal charge.
Amid the choice between ingratitude and gratitude, no burdened soul bears another's burden; inward orientation and personally borne consequence remain joined.
The scrolls of Moses and Abraham contain the maxim that no bearer bears another's burden, grounding the image of a personal load in an earlier revealed rule.
God says He gave Moses the Book and made Aaron a وَزِيرًا with him, showing the mission's weight answered by a supporting bearer alongside the prayer for inward capacity.
God recalls answering Zechariah's family prayer and says they called upon Him رَغَبًا وَرَهَبًا; desire directed into prayer supplies another form of the section's closing turn toward the Lord.
وَمَن يَرْغَبُ عَن مِّلَّةِ إِبْرَٰهِيمَ uses رغبة with عَنْ for turning away, a grammatical and moral reversal of directing it with إِلَى toward the Lord.

Abraham's father asks whether he is turning away from his gods, using رَاغِبٌ ... عَنْ; the hostile object makes especially clear how the preposition directs the root's openness away rather than toward.
Believers near Medina are forbidden to prefer their own selves over the Messenger or hold themselves back from him; رغب with عَنْ again sets self-preserving withdrawal against Godward desire.
God promises the prophetic addressee وَنُيَسِّرُكَ لِلْيُسْرَىٰ, a direct divine making-fit for ease that parallels opened capacity followed by an eased task.
The generous, God-fearing believer is promised facilitation toward ease, generalizing the section's link between receptive orientation and being made fit for the easier course.
The withholding, self-satisfied denier is facilitated toward hardship, the moral reversal that shows ease is not mere comfort but a divinely directed course.
For the three who stayed behind, the earth becomes narrow despite its breadth and their own selves become constricted; spacious surroundings cannot substitute for inward room.
God says He placed no constriction in religion and then commands striving and holding fast, pairing freedom from حَرَج with fitness for a demanding charge as the section does.
The Bedouins are told that faith has not yet entered their hearts, setting a boundary between verbal submission and the inward reception that the section's opened breast is meant to permit.
People answer the invitation by claiming their hearts are under coverings and their ears bear a weight, a precise image of blocked reception opposite to an interior opened for truth.
The claim “our hearts are wrapped” and the answer that disbelief has brought a curse present inward enclosure as the refusal opposed to an expanded breast.
God tells the Prophet that the Quran was not sent down to make him suffer, situating revealed speech as a charge for which divine aid and inward capacity are supplied.
The Prophet is promised that a weighty word will be cast upon him; this is the demanding side of revelation for which the section's opened breast and removed load make room.
God repeatedly says He made the Quran easy for remembrance, a broader scriptural instance of difficult divine speech being made accessible to receive and retain.
A parchment spread open is a plausible physical analogue for the section's dictionary action of unfolding and spreading; the ayah does not itself connect that act to the breast or to explanation.

On the traditional reading in which Abraham is told to cut the birds, their portions are distributed over the hills; this only tentatively recalls the source dictionary's cutting-and-spreading of flesh because the command's exact action is interpreted in more than one way.
